title: Arithmetic with no brackets
hook: No brackets, no 'multiply first' rule. Can a pile of numbers still get the answer right?

knows: a stack: you only add to or take from the top (back-button-stack)
doesNotKnow: that a stack can evaluate an expression written with no brackets, because the token order encodes the order of operations

misconception: Evaluating arithmetic needs brackets and precedence rules.
objective: The learner can evaluate 5 1 2 + 4 × + 3 − with a stack (1 + 2 = 3, 3 × 4 = 12, 5 + 12 = 17, 17 − 3 = 14) and say that the token order already fixes the order of operations.

claims.text: Read with a pile, 5 1 2 + 4 × + 3 − gives 1 + 2 = 3, 3 × 4 = 12, 5 + 12 = 17, 17 − 3 = 14, leaving one number: 14.
claims.source: Demo.tsx run(); builder re-ran the same stack loop in Node: [14].

claims.text: The pile was never taller than 3.
claims.source: Node: maximum stack length 3 (after 5 1 2). Demo.tsx FINAL.tallest.

claims.text: With brackets the same expression is 5 + (1 + 2) × 4 − 3.
claims.source: Rebuild the infix tree from the postfix tokens: ((5 + ((1 + 2) × 4)) − 3). Node: 5+(1+2)*4-3 = 14.

claims.text: This bracket-free way of writing is called postfix, and a stack is all it needs to evaluate.
claims.source: Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 1, 2.2.1 and 2.3.2 (postfix / reverse Polish notation, evaluated with a stack); Burks, Warren and Wright (1954) and Hamblin (1962) on the stack evaluation. Notation descends from Lukasiewicz's prefix (Polish) notation.

claims.text: An operator takes the top two numbers off and puts back their result (for −, the lower one minus the top one).
claims.source: Standard postfix evaluation rule; operand order shown on stage as '17 − 3 = 14'.

recall.question: With a pile (stack), what is 2 3 4 × + ?
recall.why: Push 2, 3, 4; × takes 3 and 4 and pushes 12; + takes 2 and 12 and pushes 14. It is 2 + 3 × 4.
